'''''Gardenia jasminoides''''', commonly known as '''gardenia''' and '''cape jasmine''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | access-date=30 November 2014}}</ref> is an [[evergreen]] [[flowering plant]] in the coffee family [[Rubiaceae]]. It is native to the [[subtropical]] and northern [[tropical]] parts of the [[Far East]]. Wild plants range from 30 centimetres to 3 metres (about 1 to 10 feet) in height. They have a rounded [[Habit (biology)|habit]] with very dense branches with opposite leaves that are lanceolate-oblong, leathery or gathered in groups on the same node and by a dark green, shiny and slightly waxy surface and prominent veins.

With its shiny green leaves and heavily fragrant white summer flowers, it is widely used in gardens in tropical, subtropical, and warm [[temperate climate|temperate]] climates. It also is used as a [[houseplant]] in temperate climates. It has been in cultivation in China for at least a thousand years, and it was introduced to [[English garden]]s in the mid-18th century. Many varieties have been bred for [[horticulture]], with low-growing, and large, and long-flowering forms.

==Description==
[[File:கும்பை8.jpg|thumb|Leaves of ''Gardenia jasminoides'']]
''Gardenia jasminoides'' is a [[shrub]] that ranges from 30 cm to 3 m (1–10 ft) high in the wild, with cylindrical to flat branches that at first are covered with [[Glossary of botanical terms|caducous]] hairs that fall early, leaving the branch smooth. The leaves are [[Phyllotaxis#Leaf arrangement|in opposite pairs]] or rarely in groups of three along the branches. They are either subsessile (almost without a petiole) or on short {{convert|0.5–1|cm|in|1|abbr=off}} petioles. The leaves themselves are {{convert|3–25|cm|in|1|abbr=on}} long by {{convert|1.5–8|cm|in|1|abbr=on}} wide and can be oblong-lanceolate, obovate-oblong, obovate, oblanceolate, or elliptic in shape. Their [[Adaxial (botany)|upper surface]] is smooth and shiny, or slightly hairy along the primary veins, while the [[Abaxial (botany)|undersurface]] is sparsely hairy to smooth. Each leaf has 8 to 15 pairs of secondary veins. The flowers are solitary and terminal, arising from the ends of the stems.<ref name=FoC>{{eFloras | 2 | 200022091| Gardenia jasminoides | family = Rubiaceae | first1 = Tao  | last1 = Chen | first2 = Xianrui  | last2 = Luo| first3= Hua| last3= Zhu| first4= Charlotte M. | last4=Taylor| first5= Friedrich | last5=Ehrendorfer | first6= Henrik | last6=Lantz | first7= Michele | last7= Funston | first8= Christian | last8=Puff | access-date = 6 January 2021 }}</ref><!-- cites para -->

The white flowers have a matte texture, in contrast to the glossy leaves. They gradually take on a creamy yellow color and a waxy surface. They can be quite large, up to {{convert|10|cm|in|abbr=on|sigfig=1}} in diameter, loosely funnel-shaped, and there are [[double-flowered]] forms. Blooming in summer and autumn, they are among the most strongly fragrant of all flowers. They are followed by small and oval fruits.<ref name="UF99">{{cite web|url=http://hort.ifas.ufl.edu/database/documents/pdf/shrub_fact_sheets/garjasa.pdf|title=Fact Sheet FPS-222: Gardenia jasminoides|last=Gilman|first=Edward F.|date=October 1999|publisher=University of Florida: Institute of food and agricultural sciences|access-date=6 June 2021|archive-date=20 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210120060100/https://hort.ifas.ufl.edu/database/documents/pdf/shrub_fact_sheets/garjasa.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>
[[File:Gardenia jasminoides fruit.jpg|thumb|Young fruit of ''Gardenia jasminoides'']]

The flowers of jasmine gardenia are all simultaneous hermaphrodites.

==Taxonomy==
German-Dutch botanist [[Georg Eberhard Rumphius|Georg Rumphius]] had seen ''Gardenia jasminoides'' on the island of Amboina ([[Ambon Island|Ambon]]), noting in his ''Herbarium Amboinense'' around 1700 that it was a "delightful ornament" called ''catsjopiri'' or ''catsjopiring'' in Malay. He reported that it had been imported there from Batavia (Jakarta).<ref name=jarvis>{{cite journal |doi=10.1111/curt.12052|title=''Gardenia jasminoides'': A Traditional Chinese Dye Plant Becomes a Garden Ornamental in Europe|year=2014|last1=Jarvis|first1=Charles E.|last2=Duval|first2=Ashley|last3=Crane|first3=Peter R.|journal=Curtis's Botanical Magazine|volume=31|pages=80–98}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Rumpf |first1=Georg Eberhard |title=Herbarium amboinense |date=1750 |publisher=Apud Fransicum Changuion, Joannem Catuffe, Hermannum Uytwerf |location=Amsterdam |pages=26–27 |url=http://botanicus.org/page/9276 |access-date=2 June 2021 |archive-date=2 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210602214812/http://botanicus.org/page/9276 |url-status=live }}</ref> Swedish taxonomist [[Carl Linnaeus]] recognized the value of Rumphius' work and assigned his student Olaf Stickman to study it. Stickman's dissertation was printed in 1754.<ref name=merrill17>{{cite book |last1=Merrill |first1=Elmer Drew |last2=Robinson |first2=Charles Budd |title=An interpretation of Rumphius's Herbarium amboinense |date=1917 |publisher=Bureau of Printing |location=Manila |pages=31–32, 485 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/44102303 |access-date=2 June 2021 |archive-date=2 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210602220447/https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/44102303 |url-status=live }}</ref> He subsequently [[species description|described]] the species as ''Varneria augusta'' in 1759.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Stickman |first1=Olaf |title=Herbarium Amboinense |journal=Amoenitates Academicae |date=1759 |volume=4 |pages=112–143 [138] |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/1484000 |access-date=2 June 2021 |archive-date=2 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210602214720/https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/1484000 |url-status=live }}</ref>

English naturalist [[John Ellis (naturalist)|John Ellis]] described ''Gardenia jasminoides'' in 1761,<ref name=Foster92>{{cite book|last=Foster|first=Steven|author2=Yue, Chongxi|title=Herbal emissaries: bringing Chinese herbs to the West: a Guide to Gardening, Herbal Wisdom, and Well-Being|publisher=Healing Arts Press|year=1992|pages=[https://archive.org/details/herbalemissaries00fost/page/185 185]|isbn=0-89281-349-0|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/herbalemissaries00fost/page/185}}</ref> having realised on dissecting the flower that it was not closely related to jasmine and warranted a new genus. He had initially proposed ''Warneria'' after the original plant's owner in England. However, Warner declined to have it named for him and so Ellis chose ''Gardenia'' to honour Scottish naturalist [[Alexander Garden (naturalist)|Alexander Garden]].<ref name=ellis1759/> Ellis had also proposed ''Augusta'' as a generic name, which Linnaeus rejected.<ref name=sprague29/> It gained its association with the name [[jasmine]] when botanist and artist [[Georg Dionysius Ehret]] depicted it. Ehret queried whether it was a jasmine because the flowers resembled the plant. The name stuck and lived on as common name and scientific epithet.<ref name=Foster92/>

Linnaeus gave it the name ''Gardenia florida'' in 1762 in the second edition of his ''[[Species Plantarum]]''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Linnaeus |first1=Carl |title=Species plantarum :exhibentes plantas rite cognitas, ad genera relatas, cum differentiis specificis, nominibus trivialibus, synonymis selectis, locis natalibus, secundum systema sexuale digestas |language=la |edition=2nd |date=1762 |volume=1 |publisher=Laurentii Salvii |location=Stockholm |page=305 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/11628759 |access-date=2 June 2021 |archive-date=2 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210602221040/https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/11628759 |url-status=live }}</ref> American botanist [[Elmer Drew Merrill|Elmer D. Merrill]] followed Stickman with ''Gardenia augusta'' in 1917;<ref name=merrill17/> however, Rumphius' original work was later deemed insufficient to describe the species, so these names are ''[[nomina nuda]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hubbard |first1=F. Tracy |last2=Rehder |first2=Alfred |title=Nomenclatorial Notes on Plants growing in the Botanical Garden of the Atkins Institution of the Arnold Arboretum at Soledad, Cienfuegos, Cuba |journal=Botanical Museum Leaflets, Harvard University |date=1932 |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=1–11 |doi=10.5962/p.295077 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/7770066 |access-date=2 June 2021 |archive-date=3 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210603051356/https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/7770066 |url-status=live |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Also based on Rumphius' work, Swedish naturalist [[Carl Peter Thunberg]] gave it the name ''Gardenia radicans'' in his 1780 work on the genus entitled ''Dissertatio botanica de Gardenia''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Thunberg |first1=Carl Peter |title=Dissertatio botanica de Gardenia |date=1780 |publisher=Johan. Edman |location=Uppsala |pages=12, 18 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/48680819}}</ref> London nurseryman [[Loddiges family|Conrad Loddiges]] described a form he had in cultivation as ''Gardenia angustifolia'' in 1821, holding it to be distinct on the basis of its narrow leaves.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Loddiges |first1=Joachim Conrad |title=The botanical cabinet |date=1821 |publisher=John & Arthur Arch |location=London |volume=6 |pages=512–513 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/29152404 |access-date=5 June 2021 |archive-date=5 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210605125551/https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/29152404 |url-status=live }}</ref>

''Gardenia jasminoides'' is highly variable in [[Morphology (biology)|morphology]], particularly in the sizes of leaves, calyx lobes and corollas in different populations. This has led to Chinese authorities describing several varieties that are not accepted elsewhere. W.C. Chen gave the name ''G. jasminoides'' var. ''fortuneana'' to a large double-flowered sterile form that does not produce seed and is widely cultivated.<ref name=FoC/>

The common names cape jasmine and cape jessamine derive from the earlier belief that the flower originated in [[Cape of Good Hope]], [[South Africa]].<ref name=Foster92/> Other common names include ''danh-danh'' and jasmin.<ref name=GRIN/>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Gardenia jasminoides'' is native to southern [[East Asia]], [[mainland Southeast Asia]], and northeastern [[South Asia]], including Nepal, Bangladesh, Cambodia, East Himalaya, Hainan, Japan, Laos, mainland China, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam,<ref name="PoWo" /> where its native habitat is forest and undergrowth along streams, and on sloping and hilly terrain to an altitude of {{Convert|1500|m|ft|abbr=off}}.<ref name="FoC" /> The species has been introduced to other areas with suitable climate and habitat, including [[Caroline Islands]], [[Comoros]], Korea, [[Mariana Islands|Marianas]], [[Marshall Islands]], [[Society Islands]] and [[Austral Islands|Tubuai Islands]].<ref name=PoWo/>

Evidence of ''G. jasminoides'' in cultivation in China dates to the [[Song dynasty]] (960–1279 AD), where both single- and double-flowered forms have been depicted in paintings, such as those of the Song emperor [[Emperor Huizong of Song|Huizong]],<ref name="Keswick">{{cite book|last=Keswick|first=Maggie|title=The Chinese Garden|publisher=Frances Lincoln| location=London|year=2003|edition=2nd|page=63|isbn=0-7112-2031-X}}</ref> and the tenth-century artist Xu Xi.<ref>Keswick, p. 204</ref> The [[Yuan dynasty]] (1271–1368) saw it on [[lacquerware]], and the [[Ming dynasty]] on porcelain (1368–1644).<ref name="Valder99">{{cite book|last=Valder|first=Peter|title=Garden Plants of China|publisher=Florilegium|location=Glebe, NSW|year=1999|page=289|isbn=1-876314-02-8}}</ref> Called ''zhi-zi'' in traditional Chinese medicine, it was a folk remedy for jaundice, oedema and fevers.<ref name=FoC/> English statesman [[Sir John Barrow, 1st Baronet|Sir John Barrow]] saw gardenias in nurseries in [[Guangzhou]], China, in 1794.<ref name="Valder99"/>

''G. jasminoides'' came to Europe via the [[Dutch Cape Colony|Cape Colony]] in southern Africa, which had been founded in 1652 as a way-station between the Netherlands and Asia. There, Daniel Des Marets, Superintendent of the Dutch estates of [[William III of England|William III]], collected material that ended up in the herbarium of English naturalist [[Hans Sloane]] in the 1680s.<ref name=jarvis/> Swedish naturalist [[Daniel Solander]] reported that the living species was brought to the United Kingdom (UK) from the Cape Colony in 1744 on the British East India Ship ''Godolphin'' by Captain William Hutchenson, who gave it to botanist [[Richard Warner (botanist)|Richard Warner]] of Woodford Row, Essex.<ref name=jarvis/><ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1098/rstl.1761.0109| title=CVII. An account of the Gardenia: In a letter to Philip Carteret Webb, Esq; F. R. S. From Daniel C. Solander, M. D| journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London| year=1761| volume=52| pages=654–661| s2cid=186210214| doi-access=free}}</ref> The plant reportedly remained in flower for much of voyage.<ref name=sprague29>{{cite journal |last1=Sprague |first1=Thomas Archibald |title=Gardenia or Warneria |journal=Bulletin of Miscellaneous Information (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew) | jstor=4115087 |date=1929 |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=12–16|doi=10.2307/4115087 }}</ref> Warner, however, was unable to propagate it until the botanist [[John Ellis (naturalist)|John Ellis]] recommended James Gordon, a gardener at [[Mile End]].<ref name=ellis1759>{{cite journal|doi=10.1098/rstl.1759.0084|title=LXXXII. An account of the plants Halesia and Gardenia: In a letter from John Ellis, Esq; F. R. S. To Philip Carteret Webb, Esq; F. R. S.|journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London| year=1759| volume=51| pages=929–935| s2cid=186210416| url=https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/pdf/10.1098/rstl.1759.0084| access-date=4 January 2021| archive-date=20 July 2020| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200720032049/https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/pdf/10.1098/rstl.1759.0084| url-status=live| url-access=subscription}}</ref> Gordon was successful in August 1757, and plants sold well thereafter.<ref name=Foster92/> Each cutting-grown plant fetched five [[Guinea (coin)|guineas]].<ref name=ellis1759/> Gardenias were first grown in the United States in 1762, in Garden's [[Charleston, South Carolina|Charleston]] garden. He had moved there 10 years previously.<ref name="Bender11">{{cite web| url=http://www.southernliving.com/home-garden/gardens/southern-gardening-gardenia-history-00400000064968/| title=A Brief History of the Gardenia| last=Bender| first=Steve| year=2011| work=Southern Living| publisher=Time Inc. Lifestyle Group| access-date=1 December 2012| location=Birmingham, AL| archive-date=17 August 2013| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130817051657/http://www.southernliving.com/home-garden/gardens/southern-gardening-gardenia-history-00400000064968/| url-status=live}}</ref>

In cultivation in the UK, ''Gardenia jasminoides'' has gained the Royal Horticultural Society's [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web|title=''Gardenia jasminoides'' AGM|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/7605/Gardenia-jasminoides/Details|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|access-date=7 July 2020|archive-date=7 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200707192422/https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/7605/Gardenia-jasminoides/Details|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants – Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 39 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 27 February 2018 | archive-date = 2 May 2020 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200502143155/https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | url-status = live }}</ref> Highly regarded for its fragrant summer flowers and attractive foliage, it is used as a specimen feature or as a hedging or screening plant.<ref name="UF99"/>

Widely used as a garden plant in warm temperate and subtropical gardens,<ref name="Bussell05"/> ''Gardenia jasminoides'' is hardy in [[USDA hardiness zone]]s 8 to 10,<ref name="UF99"/> or zone H1C in the UK (outdoor temperatures above {{convert|5|C|F|abbr=on}}).<ref name = RHSPF/> It requires good drainage and a location in a sunny or part-shaded location, and it prefers an [[Soil pH|acidic soil]] with a pH between 5.0 and 6.5.<ref name="Bussell05"/> In temperate latitudes, gardenias are usually cultivated as houseplants or in greenhouses.<ref name=rhs/> If the soil is not acidic enough, many of its nutrients (especially iron compounds) will not be available for the plant, since they will not dilute in water, so will not be absorbed by the roots. When this happens, gardenias start to develop [[chlorosis]] with the main symptom of a yellowing of the leaves.<ref>{{cite web |title=Gardenia: Common Problems |url=https://www.yates.com.au/plants/flowers-and-ornamentals/gardenia/common-problems-gardenia/ |website=Yates |publisher=DuluxGroup (Australia) Pty Ltd |access-date=21 September 2021 |archive-date=15 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210315090655/https://www.yates.com.au/plants/flowers-and-ornamentals/gardenia/common-problems-gardenia/ |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Iron chelate]] can be added to the soil to lower the pH, maybe recurrently if the water supply is [[Hard water|hard]].<ref name=rhs>{{cite web |title=Gardenia |url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/advice/profile?pid=367 |website=RHS Gardening |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 30 October 2021}}</ref>

===Cultivars===
Many [[cultivar]]s have been developed, and double-flowered forms are most popular. ''Gardenia'' 'Radicans' is a low-growing groundcover which reaches 15–45 cm (6–18 in) and spreads up to a metre wide, while ''G.'' 'Fortuniana' and ''G.'' 'Mystery' are double-flowered cultivars.<ref name="UF99"/> The former was sent by Scottish botanist [[Robert Fortune]] in 1844 to the [[Royal Horticultural Society]] in London.<ref name="Valder99"/> The latter has a large upright habit and has been a popular variety for [[Hedge|hedging]]. It reaches 1.8 to 2.5 m (6 to 8 ft) high and wide.<ref name="Bussell05">{{cite web|url=http://www.southernliving.com/home-garden/gardens/gardenias-fragrance-captivates-00400000010309/|title=Gardenias: A Fragrance That Captivates|last=Bussell|first=Gene A.|date=June 2005|work=Southern Living|publisher=Time Inc. Lifestyle Group|access-date=1 December 2012|location=Birmingham, AL|archive-date=21 October 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121021001025/http://www.southernliving.com/home-garden/gardens/gardenias-fragrance-captivates-00400000010309/|url-status=live}}</ref> Unlike other varieties, ''G.'' 'Golden Magic' bears flowers which change to a golden yellow relatively early after opening white. It grows to 1.5 m (5 ft) high and 1 m (3.5 ft) wide.<ref name="Plantmark">{{cite web|url=http://plantmark.com.au/gardenias.html |title=Gardenias |last=Plantmark |year=2006 |publisher=self |access-date=1 December 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130410181648/http://plantmark.com.au/gardenias.html |archive-date=10 April 2013 }}</ref>

==Uses<span class="anchor" id="Traditional uses"></span>==
Gardenia flowers can be eaten raw, pickled, or preserved in honey.{{Citation needed|date=October 2021}} In China, the petals are used in tea for their aroma, while a yellow-red dye used in textiles and sweets has been extracted from the pulp of the fruit.<ref name=jarvis/> ''Gardenia jasminoides fructus'' (fruit) is used in [[traditional Chinese medicine]] to "drain fire" and treat certain [[Fever|febrile]] conditions. It has anti-inflammatory and antipyretic effects.<ref>{{cite book | author =Bensky, Dan| title = Chinese Herbal Medicine Materia Medica | edition = 3rd | publisher = Eastland Press, Inc | location =Seattle | date = 2004 | page = 95|display-authors=etal}}</ref>

Shishihakuhito is a Chinese herbal medicine mainly composed of gardenia fruit and is used to treat [[atopic dermatitis]]. It inhibits [[Immunoglobulin E]] (IgE) mediated histamine release.<ref name="shishi">{{Cite journal |author=Mie Wakabayashi |author2=Eiko Sakurai |author3=Kazuhiko Yanai |author4=Kazuhiro Umemura |author5=Masaaki Yoshida |author6=Yasushi Ohizumi |author7=Tohru Yamakuni |date=2009 |title=Shishihakuhito, a traditional Chinese medicine for atopic dermatitis, inhibits IgE-mediated histamine release from rat RBL-2H3 basophilic leukocyte cells |journal=Journal of Traditional Medicines |volume=26 |pages=44–49 |doi=10.11339/jtm.26.44 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

In 2020, a case of someone who had developed blue-gray discoloration of the skin as a result of chronic intake of gardenia fruit extract was published.<ref name="blue">{{Cite journal |last1=Mizawa |first1=Megumi |last2=Andoh |first2=Tsugunobu |last3=Shimizu |first3=Tadamichi |date=2020-03-01 |title=Gardenia Fruit–Related Blue-Gray Skin Pigmentation |url=https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamadermatology/fullarticle/2759771 |journal=JAMA Dermatology |language=en |volume=156 |issue=3 |pages=351–353 |doi=10.1001/jamadermatol.2019.4682 |pmid=32022833 |s2cid=211037594 |issn=2168-6068|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===Chemistry===
{{As of|2020}}, at least 162 compounds have been identified in ''Gardenia jasminoides''.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2020.112829|title=Gardenia jasminoides Ellis: Ethnopharmacology, phytochemistry, and pharmacological and industrial applications of an important traditional Chinese medicine|year=2020|last1=Chen|first1=Liping|last2=Li|first2=Maoxing|last3=Yang|first3=Zhiqiang|last4=Tao|first4=Wendi|last5=Wang|first5=Peng|last6=Tian|first6=Xiuyu|last7=Li|first7=Xiaolin|last8=Wang|first8=Weigang|journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology|volume=257|article-number=112829|pmid=32311486|s2cid=216047427}}</ref> The [[iridoid]]s [[genipin]] and [[geniposidic acid]] can be found in ''G. jasminoides'' fruit.<ref>{{cite journal | pmid = 16169698 | year = 2006 | last1 = Koo | first1 = HJ | last2 = Lim | first2 = KH | last3 = Jung | first3 = HJ | last4 = Park | first4 = EH | title = Anti-inflammatory evaluation of gardenia extract, geniposide and genipin | volume = 103 | issue = 3 | pages = 496–500 | doi = 10.1016/j.jep.2005.08.011 | journal = Journal of Ethnopharmacology}}</ref>

[[Crocetin]], a chemical compound usually obtained from ''[[Crocus sativus]]'', also can be obtained from the fruit of ''Gardenia jasminoides''.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Yamauchi | first1 = M | last2 = Tsuruma | first2 = K | last3 = Imai | first3 = S | last4 = Nakanishi | first4 = T | last5 = Umigai | first5 = N | last6 = Shimazawa | first6 = M | last7 = Hara | first7 = H | title = Crocetin prevents retinal degeneration induced by oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum stresses via inhibition of caspase activity | journal = European Journal of Pharmacology | volume = 650 | issue = 1 | pages = 110–9 | year = 2011 | pmid = 20951131 | doi = 10.1016/j.ejphar.2010.09.081}}</ref> The fully matured fruit were found to contain [[crocin]] in a concentration of 4.5 mg of total crocetin derivatives per gram (dry weight), and can be used as a yellow dye<ref name="Valder99"/> to color clothing and food.<ref>{{cite journal | year = 1995 | last1 = Ichi | first1 = T | last2 = Higashimura | first2 = Y | last3 = Katayama | first3 = T | last4 = Koda | first4 = T | last5 = Shimizu | first5 = T | last6 = Tada | first6 = M | title = Analysis of Crocetin Derivatives from Gardenia | volume = 42 | issue = 10 | pages = 776–783 | doi = 10.3136/nskkk.42.776 | journal = Nippon Shokuhin Kagaku Kogaku Kaishi| s2cid = 87600533 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

== Cultural significance ==

=== Buddhism ===
Gardenia flowers are commonly used as floral offerings at [[Buddhist temple]]s in [[Tropical Asia]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Xinyang |last2=Jin |first2=Cheng |last3=Huang |first3=Li |last4=Zhou |first4=Lihua |last5=Zheng |first5=Mingming |last6=Qian |first6=Shenhua |last7=Yang |first7=Yongchuan |title=Plant diversity and species replacement in Chinese Buddhist temples |journal=Biodiversity Science |date=2020-06-20 |volume=28 |issue=6 |page=668 |doi=10.17520/biods.2019392|doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Japanese Shogi and Go ===
The legs of seated-style [[Shogi]] and [[Go (game)|Go]] boards from [[Japan]] are traditionally carved in the image of gardenia fruits. In the [[Japanese language]], "gardenia" (''kuchinashi'', くちなし) is a [[homophone]] of "no mouth" (''kuchinashi'', 口無し). This symbolizes that neither players nor spectators are allowed to speak during a game.<ref>{{Citation |title=How to play Shogi(将棋) -Lesson#38- Shogi Board as Arts and Crafts | date=17 January 2009 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h9zb5udfeWo&list=PL587865CAE59EB84A |language=en |access-date=2022-12-26}}</ref>
[[File:Go-tisch.png|none|thumb|330x330px|Japanese [[Go (game)|Go]] board showing legs in the shape of gardenia fruits.]]

=== Meitei culture ===
{{See|Meitei culture}}
Giving reference to [[Meitei people|Meitei]] King [[Khagemba]] and the [[Manipur Kingdom]], the beauty and grace of [[Kaboklei|Lei Kabok]], also called {{lang|mni|Kabok Lei}} ({{lang|la|Gardenia jasminoides}}<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-10-31 |title=Kaboklei |url=https://medicinalplants.co.in/kaboklei/ |access-date=2023-04-10 |website=Manipur Medicinal Plants |language=en-US}}</ref>), is described by Meitei King [[Charairongba]], in his literary work, "Leiron" ({{langx|mni|{{Script|Mtei|ꯂꯩꯔꯣꯟ}}}}) which is an account on the description of 100 flowers and orchids, endemic as well as exotic species in [[Kangleipak]],<ref>{{Cite book |last=Singh |first=Ch Manihar |title=A History of Manipuri Literature |date=1996 |publisher=[[Sahitya Akademi]] |isbn=978-81-260-0086-9 |page=96 |language=en, mni}}</ref> as follows:
{{Quote|It is a flower that remains ever fresh as not eaten by worms and is fondly sought after in the four corners of [[Manipur Kingdom|the country]], eight directions, nay in all quarters. It is distinct for its beautiful shape, its tender stalk and for its pure white colour. It is a flower once nurtured by King [[Khagemba]] who preferred to take it with him even for his long home. It is a flower that comes handy to both boys and girls as a present of love. Such a luscious flower has blossomed forth in an unending array of white and definitely the season is of this flower.|Leiron|[[Charairongba]]<ref>{{Cite book |last=Singh |first=Ch Manihar |title=A History of Manipuri Literature |date=1996 |publisher=[[Sahitya Akademi]] |isbn=978-81-260-0086-9 |pages=92, 93 |language=en, mni}}</ref>}}
